concept.name: Spearman rank correlation
concept.definition: A nonparametric measure of monotonic association between two variables, defined as the Pearson correlation coefficient computed on the ranks of the observations rather than their raw values. It ranges from -1 to +1 and detects any consistent monotonic relationship, linear or not.
concept.intuition: It asks 'do bigger x values reliably come with bigger y values?' regardless of how big the steps are. Only the ordering matters, so outliers can do no more damage than their rank allows.
concept.mechanics: Rank each variable separately (averaging ranks for ties), then compute the Pearson correlation of the rank pairs. With no ties, a simplified formula in the squared rank differences d_i applies; with ties, the general Pearson-on-ranks form must be used.
concept.formula: rs = 1 - 6*SUM(d_i^2) / (n*(n^2 - 1)), where d_i is the difference between the two ranks of observation i and n is the sample size; valid only when all ranks are distinct (no ties).
concept.failure_modes: The simplified d^2 formula gives wrong values when ties are present. Like all correlation measures it does not imply causation, and it quantifies monotone association only - a non-monotonic (e.g., inverted-U) dependence can score near zero. With small samples, significance is hard to establish.
concept.misconceptions: A perfect Spearman coefficient does not require a linear relationship - any strictly monotonic one gives +/-1, so Spearman = 1 is weaker evidence than Pearson = 1. Nor is Spearman simply 'Pearson with outliers removed'; it answers a different question (monotonic vs. linear).
concept.example: Ranking 10 people by IQ and by weekly TV hours yields SUM d_i^2 = 58 and n = 10, giving rho = 1 - 6*58/(10*99) = -0.176, a weak negative monotonic association.
